title: Redis Caching Patterns: Scaling Backend Architecture ⚡
ig_caption:
Redis caching patterns: scaling backend architecture—how memory leaks happen in real systems? ⚡
Cache aside, heap growth, GC, and why your server crashes.

• The heap is where your server stores live objects (and dreams)
• Requests come in → caching grows (or never shrinks)
• Cache keeps every user → unbounded keys = memory climb
• GC cleanup exists, but it only frees unreachable objects
• “Leak” often means references stay reachable (maps, queues, listeners)
• RAM limit gets hit → heap fragmentation → GC thrash → blocked requests

Practical takeaway: In interviews, ask “Where do keys expire? Who holds references?” Then quantify cardinality + TTL.

Debate: Is your “memory leak” really a GC problem—or an architectural retention problem?

Redis caching patterns: scaling backend architecture—and the hidden path from “in-memory cache” to a real memory leak.

What people call a “memory leak” is often retention by design:

- Unbounded cache cardinality: cache keeps every user (and every session attribute) → key explosion
- Cache-aside gotchas: if misses fall back to DB but write-backs never expire, memory monotonically grows
- Reachability beats GC: garbage collection only reclaims objects that are unreachable; if your cache, maps, or event listeners still reference them, GC can’t help
- Backpressure and blocked work: when the heap hits RAM limits, GC thrash increases pause time and request handling can effectively stall
- Heap growth vs. fragmentation: even with “cleanup,” allocator churn can degrade latency until the server crashes

Production patterns that prevent this:
- Enforce TTLs and eviction policies (LRU/LFU) and set sane max-memory bounds
- Use key design with strict limits (avoid per-user-per-request keys unless absolutely necessary)
- Add observability: heap usage, live-set size, GC time, cache hit ratio, and key counts
- Validate reference lifetimes: look for long-lived maps, listeners, and queues that retain objects
